title: Chemical bonds: how atoms hold on to each other

summary.text: Boil water and the steam drips back off a lid as water. A small battery can do what boiling cannot: split water into two gases, hydrogen and oxygen. Water is made of atoms that hold on to each other very tightly. This holding is called a chemical bond, and it is made by the atoms' electrons. Every solid, liquid and gas around us, and every part of you, is atoms held by bonds.
summary.art: A glass of water with two pencils standing in it, wires going to a small battery, and streams of tiny bubbles rising from both pencil tips.

intro.hook: Next time someone cooks rice or boils milk, look under the lid. It is covered in drops. Touch one. It is plain water. The water went up as steam and came back as water.
intro.text: So heating moves water around, but it does not change water into something else. Is water a single, simple stuff that can never be broken? People thought so for over two thousand years. In this unit you will split water yourself, with a pencil and a battery, and find out what it is made of.
intro.art: A steel lid held up over a pot of rice, with drops of water hanging on its underside and a child's finger touching one.

outcomes: I can say what a chemical bond is: atoms holding on to each other, using their electrons.
I can say what a molecule is, and build models of water, oxygen and carbon dioxide.
I can say how many bonds hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and carbon usually make, and use this to explain why water is H2O.
I can split water into two gases with a battery, and explain why boiling cannot do this.
I can tell a change where molecules only move apart (melting, boiling, dissolving) from a change where atoms let go and make new bonds (cooking, burning, rusting).
I can explain why pencil lead is soft but diamond is hard, though both are made only of carbon.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece of an element. Everything around you is made of atoms, far too small to see.
terms.example: One drop of water holds more than a thousand billion billion atoms.
terms.art: A drop of water on a leaf with a magnifying circle showing a neat pattern of tiny balls inside.

terms.meaning: A substance made of only one kind of atom. There are 118 known elements.
terms.example: Oxygen, hydrogen, carbon, iron and gold are elements.
terms.art: Five small jars labelled oxygen, hydrogen, carbon, iron and gold, each with one kind of ball inside.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle with a negative electric charge, found on the outside of every atom. Electrons make the bonds between atoms.
terms.example: When two atoms share a pair of electrons, both atoms hold on to that pair.
terms.art: An atom drawn as a small centre with a fuzzy cloud of dots around it.

terms.meaning: The way two atoms hold on to each other. Their electrons are attracted by both atoms at once, so the atoms stay together.
terms.example: In water, each hydrogen atom has one bond with the oxygen atom.
terms.art: Two balls, one big and one small, joined by a short stick, with a faint cloud around the join.

terms.meaning: A group of atoms held together by bonds. It is the smallest piece of a substance like water or sugar.
terms.example: A water molecule is one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms held on to it.
terms.art: A big red ball with two small white balls stuck on, like a head with two ears.

terms.meaning: A substance made of two or more kinds of atom held together by bonds.
terms.example: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Sugar is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
terms.art: A water molecule and a sugar molecule side by side, with different colours for each kind of atom.

terms.meaning: The lightest element. A hydrogen atom usually makes one bond. Hydrogen gas burns easily.
terms.example: In your experiment, the bubbles at the pencil joined to the minus side of the battery were hydrogen.
terms.art: A tiny white ball with one short stick, like a hand, held out.

terms.meaning: An element. The oxygen gas in air is what we breathe in. An oxygen atom usually makes two bonds.
terms.example: Air has oxygen molecules, each made of two oxygen atoms held together.
terms.art: Two red balls held together by two short sticks.

terms.meaning: An element. A carbon atom usually makes four bonds. Diamond and pencil lead are both pure carbon.
terms.example: Carbon is in sugar, in wood, in rice and in every living thing.
terms.art: A black ball with four short sticks pointing out, like a jack.

terms.meaning: Splitting a substance using electricity. Electro means electricity, and lysis means splitting.
terms.example: A 9-volt battery and two pencils split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
terms.art: A battery joined by wires to two pencils standing in a glass, with bubbles at the tips.

terms.meaning: A change where atoms let go of their partners and make new bonds, so a new substance is made. It is often hard to undo.
terms.example: Sugar heated on a spoon turns into brown caramel, which does not turn back into white sugar.
terms.art: A steel spoon with white sugar on one side and brown caramel on the other, with an arrow between.

terms.meaning: A change where molecules move apart or closer, but each molecule stays whole. No new substance is made.
terms.example: Ice melting into water, and water boiling into steam, are physical changes.
terms.art: An ice cube, a puddle and a cloud of steam in a row, each showing the same little water molecules.

terms.meaning: A soft, grey form of carbon. Its atoms are held in flat sheets that slide over each other. Pencil lead is graphite mixed with clay.
terms.example: When you write, sheets of graphite slide off the pencil and stay on the paper.
terms.art: A pencil tip on paper, with a zoomed circle showing flat sheets of carbon rings sliding off.

explanations.context: This card says what holds atoms together. Remember the water-splitting test: the battery had to work to pull water's atoms apart.
explanations.definition: A chemical bond is the way two atoms hold on to each other. It is made by electrons, which are attracted by both atoms at once.
explanations.description: Every atom has a centre with a positive electric charge, and electrons around it with a negative charge. Opposite charges attract. When two atoms come close, some of their electrons are attracted by both centres at once. So the two atoms stay together. Nothing like glue or hooks is involved. The holding is the electric force.
examples: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom shares a pair of electrons with each hydrogen atom. Those two shared pairs are the two bonds.
The oxygen you breathe is two oxygen atoms bonded together. They stay paired as they float in the air.
explanations.art: Two atoms close together, each with a plus sign in the centre, and a pair of small dots between them, with arrows from both centres to the dots.

explanations.concept: Molecules: atoms held in a group
explanations.context: This card is about the small groups of atoms that make up water, air and sugar.
explanations.definition: A molecule is a group of atoms held together by bonds. It is the smallest piece of a substance like water.
explanations.description: Scientists write a molecule with letters and small numbers. H stands for hydrogen, O for oxygen, C for carbon and N for nitrogen. H2O means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. So one drop of water is a huge crowd of H2O molecules. Each molecule is the same, wherever the water came from.
examples: Carbon dioxide, the gas you breathe out: CO2, 3 atoms.
Table sugar: C12H22O11, 45 atoms in one molecule.
explanations.art: Three molecule models in a row: a water molecule, a carbon dioxide molecule in a straight line, and a big sugar molecule with many balls.

explanations.concept: Each kind of atom has a set number of bonds
explanations.context: This card explains why water is H2O, and not HO or H3O.
explanations.definition: Each kind of atom usually makes the same number of bonds. Hydrogen makes 1, oxygen makes 2, nitrogen makes 3 and carbon makes 4.
explanations.description: Think of bonds as hands. Hydrogen has one hand, oxygen two, nitrogen three and carbon four. In a molecule, every hand is held by another atom's hand. Oxygen has two hands, so it holds two hydrogens. That makes H2O. Sometimes two atoms hold each other with two hands, or even three. This is called a double or triple bond.
examples: Methane, the main gas in biogas and in piped cooking gas: one carbon holding four hydrogens, CH4.
Carbon dioxide: one carbon holds each oxygen with two hands, so all four of its hands are used.
Nitrogen gas, most of the air: two nitrogen atoms holding each other with all three hands.
explanations.art: Four balls with sticks for hands: white hydrogen with 1, red oxygen with 2, blue nitrogen with 3, black carbon with 4.

explanations.concept: Two kinds of holding: inside a molecule and between molecules
explanations.context: This card explains the main result of the water-splitting test: why boiling cannot split water, but a battery can.
explanations.definition: Bonds hold the atoms inside a molecule together very strongly. Molecules also pull on each other, but much more weakly.
explanations.description: When ice melts, or water boils, the weak pulls between molecules give way. The molecules move further apart, but each one stays whole H2O. That is why steam drips back from a lid as water. Splitting the molecule itself means breaking the strong bonds inside it. It takes several times more energy than boiling the same water away. Your battery gave that energy, a little at a time.
examples: Ice, water and steam are all H2O molecules. Only the spacing and movement changes.
Sugar dissolving in water: the sugar molecules move apart among the water molecules, but each sugar molecule stays whole.
explanations.art: Three boxes: ice with molecules packed in a pattern, water with them close but jumbled, steam with them far apart. Each molecule is a red ball with two white balls.

explanations.concept: Breaking and making bonds makes new substances
explanations.context: This card is about cooking, burning and rusting, and what happens to bonds in them.
explanations.definition: In a chemical change, atoms let go of some partners and make bonds with new ones. The atoms are all still there, but they now form new substances.
explanations.description: No atom is made or destroyed in a chemical change. The same atoms are just joined in a new way. Breaking bonds takes in energy. Making new bonds gives energy out. A gas flame is hot because the gas's atoms make new, strong bonds with oxygen from the air. The new molecules are carbon dioxide and water.
examples: Sugar heated on a spoon breaks down and forms brown caramel. Some of its hydrogen and oxygen atoms leave as steam.
An iron gate rusts: iron atoms bond with oxygen, with help from water, and make brown rust.
A dosa turns golden brown on the tava, as molecules in the batter break and join in new ways.
explanations.art: A pan with a golden dosa, a rusty balcony grill and a blue gas flame, each with a small circle showing atoms joined in new pairs.

explanations.concept: Same atoms, different bonds: pencil lead and diamond
explanations.context: This card shows that how atoms are bonded matters as much as which atoms they are.
explanations.definition: Graphite and diamond are both made only of carbon atoms. They are different because their atoms are bonded in different patterns.
explanations.description: In diamond, every carbon atom holds four others in every direction, so the whole crystal is one strong frame. Diamond is the hardest natural material. In graphite, each carbon atom holds three others in a flat sheet. The sheets lie on top of each other and hold on only weakly. So they slide apart easily, and leave a grey mark on paper.
examples: A pencil leaves a mark because sheets of graphite slide off onto the paper.
Diamond-tipped tools cut glass and stone, because no natural material is harder.
explanations.art: Left: a diamond with a zoomed view of a 3D frame of carbon atoms. Right: a pencil with a zoomed view of flat sheets stacked like pages.

explanations.context: This card explains the third experiment: why soda water made many bubbles but sugar water made very few.
explanations.definition: Water carries the battery's electricity well only when it has charged particles dissolved in it.
explanations.description: Cooking soda and salt are not made of molecules. They are made of particles with electric charges, held together by their opposite charges. In water, these charged particles move apart and can drift towards the battery's wires. That carries the electricity across. Sugar dissolves as whole molecules with no charge. So sugar water carries almost no electricity, and very little water splits.
examples: Soda water makes many bubbles in the water-splitting test. Salt water does too, but it also makes a little chlorine gas, so we do not use it at home.
Pure water, and sugar water, make very few bubbles with a 9-volt battery.
explanations.art: Two glasses: one with plus and minus dots drifting towards two pencils and many bubbles, one with plain sugar molecules and almost no bubbles.

explanations.context: This card is about a question chemists still argue about: is a bond a real thing, or a way of describing atoms?
explanations.description: We draw bonds as sticks. But no atom has a stick. Electrons spread round atoms as a cloud, not as little dots in a line. Since 2009, special microscopes have made pictures of single molecules where the bonds show up as lines. People still disagree about what those lines are.
examples: In 1955, the chemist Charles Coulson wrote that no one has ever seen a bond, and that it is an idea people made up.
In 2009, scientists at IBM in Zurich made a picture of one pentacene molecule, and its bonds showed up as lines.

perspectives.explanation: A bond is real. You can measure its length and how much energy it takes to break. You can now see it in pictures.
Only atoms and electrons are real. A bond is a useful way of describing where the electrons gather. It is not a separate thing.

explanations.art: A fuzzy grey picture of a molecule with five rings in a row, next to a drawing of the same molecule with neat stick bonds.

agreed.text: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen, not an element. Each molecule is H2O.
agreed.evidence: Water can be split by electricity into hydrogen and oxygen, with twice as much hydrogen as oxygen. Burning hydrogen in oxygen makes water again.

agreed.text: Chemical bonds are made by electrons, held by the electric force.
agreed.evidence: Bonds can be measured and calculated from the way electrons and atomic centres attract. The calculations match experiments.

agreed.text: Melting, boiling and dissolving move molecules apart without breaking the bonds inside them.
agreed.evidence: Steam turns back into water, and dissolved sugar can be dried back into sugar. The molecules were whole all along.

agreed.text: In a chemical change, no atoms are made or lost. They only change partners.
agreed.evidence: Antoine Lavoisier and later scientists weighed everything before and after reactions in closed containers. The total weight stays the same.

agreed.text: Each kind of atom usually makes a set number of bonds: hydrogen 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3, carbon 4.
agreed.evidence: Thousands of molecules have been measured, and almost all of them follow these numbers.

challenging.claim: Water is an element, one of the basic stuffs everything is made of.
challenging.who: Greek and Indian thinkers for over 2,000 years, and most scientists until the 1780s
challenging.for: Water never seems to change into anything else. Freeze it, boil it or mix it, and you get water back.
challenging.against: In 1800, Nicholson and Carlisle split water into hydrogen and oxygen with a battery. You can do it at home.
challenging.context: This card is about one of the oldest ideas in science, and how it was shown wrong.

challenging.claim: Boiling water splits it into hydrogen and oxygen.
challenging.who: A common guess, because both are gases
challenging.for: Water turns into a gas when it boils.
challenging.against: Steam caught on a cold lid turns back into water. If it were hydrogen and oxygen, it would not.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mix-up between boiling and splitting.

challenging.claim: Atoms are held together by tiny hooks.
challenging.who: Some ancient Greek and Roman thinkers, such as the poet Lucretius
challenging.for: Things stick together, so something must catch hold.
challenging.against: Atoms have no hooks. Bonds are made by electrons, held by the electric force.
challenging.context: This card is about an old picture of how atoms join.

challenging.claim: A chemical bond is a real thing, as real as an atom.
challenging.who: Many chemists, while some physicists and philosophers disagree
challenging.for: Bonds have lengths and strengths that can be measured. They show up as lines in pictures from special microscopes.
challenging.against: What is really there is atoms and their electrons. A bond is our name for where the electrons gather.
challenging.context: This card is about a question chemists still argue about.

challenging.claim: When something burns, its atoms are destroyed.
challenging.who: A common idea, because ash weighs less than the wood
challenging.for: A log turns into a small heap of ash.
challenging.against: Most of the wood's atoms go into the air as carbon dioxide and water. Catch the gases and weigh them, and nothing is lost.
challenging.context: This card is about where the atoms go in a fire.

big_questions.q: Water's atoms hold on so tightly that boiling cannot pull them apart. What would the world be like if bonds were as weak as the pulls between molecules?
big_questions.hint: Think of what would happen to your body, your food and the rocks on a hot day.

big_questions.q: Diamond and pencil lead are both pure carbon. Is a diamond a different thing from a pencil, or the same thing arranged differently?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to change to turn one into the other?

big_questions.q: Nobody has ever seen a bond, only atoms close together. Is a bond a thing, or a name for how atoms behave?
big_questions.hint: Is a handshake a thing, or two hands doing something?

big_questions.q: Some of the oxygen you breathe in ends up inside you as part of water. Where does the air end and you begin?
big_questions.hint: Your body uses oxygen from air to get energy from food, and makes water and carbon dioxide.

big_questions.q: Every atom in you was once part of other things, held by other bonds. What does it mean for an atom to belong to you?
big_questions.hint: Think of the rice you ate yesterday. Where are its atoms now?

big_questions.q: Atoms of only about 25 elements make up a human body. How can so few kinds make so many different things?
big_questions.hint: Think of how 26 letters make every word in English.

story.title: Bubbles That Were Not Steam
story.note: A made-up story. The water-splitting test in it is the one in this unit.
text: It was the morning of Pongal in Madurai. On the balcony of the flat, Paati had tied fresh turmeric leaves round the neck of the new pot. The milk in it was rising. Kavya, who was ten, held her little brother Arjun back from the stove.
The milk frothed over the side. 'Pongalo pongal!' everyone shouted. Paati added the rice and covered the pot with a steel lid.
Later, when Paati lifted the lid, Arjun pointed. 'Look, it is raining under the lid.' Big drops hung all over it. One dripped onto his hand. It was warm, and it was only water.
'The water in the pot went up as steam,' said Paati. 'The cold lid turned it back into water.'
Arjun thought about this while they ate. 'So when water boils, it is still water,' he said. 'And when it freezes, it is still water. Water is always water. You can never break it.'
'Are you sure?' said Kavya. She was smiling in a way that made Arjun suspicious.
'Sure,' he said. 'I have seen water go up, and come down, and turn into ice. It always comes back.'

After lunch, Kavya came out of her room with a small box. In it were two pencils, a nine-volt battery with a clip on two wires, and a strip of cardboard. Their aunt, Revathi Chithi, who mends phones and radios, had shown her this last summer.

Kavya sharpened both pencils at both ends. She pushed them through two holes in the cardboard and laid it across a glass of water. She stirred in a spoon of cooking soda. Then she twisted one wire round the top of each pencil.
'Now watch the bottom of the pencils,' she said.
At first, nothing. Then a thin line of bubbles began to rise from one pencil tip. A few seconds later, the other tip began to bubble too.
'It is boiling!' said Arjun.
'Touch the glass,' said Kavya.
He did. It was cool. The water was not even warm.
'Then what are the bubbles?' he asked.
'Gases that come out of the water,' said Kavya. 'Look closely. Which pencil makes more?'
Arjun put his nose almost on the glass. 'This one. The one with the black wire.'
Kavya swapped the wires round. Now the other pencil made more bubbles. 'So it is not the pencil,' Arjun said slowly. 'It is the black wire. The minus side.'
'Chithi told me the black side makes hydrogen,' said Kavya. 'The red side makes oxygen. Water is made of those two. Every tiny bit of water is one oxygen and two hydrogens, holding on tight.'
'Two hydrogens,' said Arjun. 'That is why there are more bubbles on that side!'
Kavya had not thought of that. She looked at the bubbles again. There were about twice as many on the black side. 'I think you are right,' she said.
Paati had come to the door. 'So the steam on my lid was not broken water?'

'No, Paati,' said Arjun, before Kavya could answer. 'Boiling only makes the water bits fly apart from each other. The bits stay whole, so they come back as water. The battery breaks the bits themselves.'
Paati laughed. 'Then all those years I called water the simplest thing in the kitchen, it was two gases holding hands.'
That evening, Arjun drew a picture for Revathi Chithi. It showed a glass, two pencils and many bubbles. Under it he wrote, in large letters: WATER CAN BE BROKEN. BUT NOT BY BOILING.
story.epiphany: For the parent: boiling only separates water molecules from each other, so steam turns back into water. The battery breaks the bonds inside each molecule, making two new gases, hydrogen and oxygen. There is twice as much hydrogen because each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms.
ask: Why did the drops under the lid turn out to be water, and not something new?
How did Arjun know the bubbles were not from boiling?
Why did Kavya swap the wires, and what did it show?
Why were there more bubbles on one side?

games.title: Hold Every Hand: an atom card game
games.context: This is a card game about bonds. Each atom card shows how many hands that atom has. You score by building molecules where every hand is held.

printables.title: 8 molecule cards (the atoms are on the back)

items.b: 2 H and 1 O. 3 points.
2 H. 2 points.
2 O, holding each other with both hands. 2 points.
1 C and 2 O. Carbon holds each O with two hands. 3 points.
1 C and 4 H. 5 points.
1 N and 3 H. 4 points.
2 N, holding each other with all three hands. 2 points.
2 H and 2 O, in a chain H, O, O, H. 4 points.

rules: Lay the 8 molecule cards in a row with the name side up. Keep the atoms on the back hidden.
Shuffle the 30 atom cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down as the pile.
On your turn, take the top card of the pile.
Then you may build one molecule from your cards. Say its name, and lay down the atoms with every hand held. If two atoms hold each other with two or three hands, overlap their cards.
Turn the molecule card over to check the atoms. If you are right, score the points on the back. If you are wrong, take your cards back and score nothing.
After building, take cards from the pile until you have 5 again. If you did not build, put one card from your hand face up in a used pile, so you have 5.
When the pile is empty, finish the round. Most points wins. A tie is a shared win.

setup.art: Small paper cards with H, O, N and C written on them, each with the right number of little hands drawn round the letter.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the atom cards. Each shows its number of hands.

setup.art: Three cards laid on a table, an O card in the middle and two H cards touching it, making water.
setup.caption: 2. Build a molecule where every hand is held. Check the back of its card and score the points.

flow.do: 1. Print or draw the atom cards. 2. Lay out one card of each kind.
flow.say: Each atom has a set number of hands. Count them on each card.
flow.kid: Look at each card. Count the hands. Hydrogen has 1. Oxygen has 2. Nitrogen has 3. Carbon has 4.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hold Every Hand. You learn how many bonds each atom makes.

flow.do: Build water together. Put one O card and two H cards next to each other.
flow.say: Oxygen has two hands. How many hydrogens can it hold?
flow.kid: Put one O in the middle. How many H cards can it hold? Try it.

ask.q: Why not three hydrogens on one oxygen?
good: There would be no hand for the third one.

check.q: Oxygen has 2 hands and hydrogen has 1. How many hydrogens does one oxygen hold?
check.why: Each of oxygen's two hands holds one hydrogen's hand. So one oxygen holds two hydrogens, and that is H2O, water. Picking 1 leaves one oxygen hand empty. Picking 4 needs four hands, and oxygen has only two.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules. Take turns.
flow.say: Your turn. Can you build something where every hand is held?
flow.kid: Take a card. Can you build a molecule? Every hand must be held. Lay it down and count your atoms.
flow.parent: Carbon dioxide is the hardest. Carbon holds each oxygen with two hands. Lay two cards overlapping to show a double hold.

flow.do: Add up the scores.
flow.say: Who has the most points? Which molecule was the hardest to build?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which molecule was hardest?
flow.think: Carbon has four hands. What is the biggest molecule you could build with one carbon?

games.title: Same Stuff or New Stuff? a sorting card game
games.context: This is a card game about changes. For each change, players decide: did the molecules only move apart, or did atoms make new bonds and a new substance?

printables.title: 16 change cards (the answer is on the back)

items.f: An ice cube melts in a tumbler
items.b: Same stuff. Water molecules move apart a little.
Same stuff. Water molecules fly apart as steam.
Same stuff. Sugar molecules spread among water molecules.

items.f: Ghee melts in a hot pan
items.b: Same stuff. It turns solid again when cool.

items.f: Steam turns to drops on a lid
items.b: Same stuff. Water molecules come close again.

items.f: A candle's wax melts and drips
items.b: Same stuff. The drips harden into wax again.

items.f: Wet clothes dry on the line
items.b: Same stuff. Water molecules leave into the air.

items.f: Butter goes soft in the sun
items.b: Same stuff. Its molecules move more freely.

items.f: Sugar turns brown on a hot spoon
items.b: New stuff. Sugar breaks down and makes caramel.
New stuff. Its atoms bond with oxygen and make smoke, gases and ash.
New stuff. Iron bonds with oxygen and makes rust.
New stuff. Bacteria change milk sugar into a new acid, and milk proteins clump.

items.f: Dosa batter turns golden on the tava
items.b: New stuff. Molecules in the batter break and join in new ways.

items.f: A gas stove burns with a blue flame
items.b: New stuff. The gas bonds with oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and water.

items.f: A battery splits water into bubbles
items.b: New stuff. Hydrogen and oxygen gas.

items.f: A green banana turns yellow and sweet
items.b: New stuff. The banana changes starch into sugar.

rules: Shuffle the 16 change cards and put them face down.
Take turns to pick the top card. Read the front aloud, and keep the back hidden.
Everyone except the reader holds up a sign: Same stuff or New stuff.
The reader turns the card and checks. Everyone who was right gets a point.
The reader then explains why, using the back. A good reason earns the reader an extra point.
The game ends when all 16 cards are read. Most points wins. With two players, one reads and the other guesses, then swap.

setup.art: A pile of cut-out cards, one turned over showing a picture of an ice cube melting in a tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Turn over a card and read the change.

setup.art: Two family members holding up signs, one saying SAME STUFF and one saying NEW STUFF.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone except the reader holds up a sign. Then check the back.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Make two signs, Same stuff and New stuff.
flow.say: In some changes, the molecules only move apart. In others, atoms make new bonds. Let's see if we can tell.
flow.kid: Make two signs. Same stuff. New stuff.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Same Stuff or New Stuff game. You sort changes by what happens to the bonds.

flow.do: Play by the rules, taking turns to read.
flow.say: What do you think? Same stuff, or new stuff? Why?
flow.kid: Read your card. Hold up a sign. Then say why.

ask.q: How can you tell new stuff was made?
good: It does not go back when you cool it.
It has a new colour or smell.

flow.parent: A useful test is: could you get the first thing back just by cooling, warming or drying? If yes, it is usually the same stuff.

flow.do: Count the points.
flow.say: Which card made us argue most?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card was hardest?

check.q: Melted ghee turns solid again in the fridge. What does that tell you?
check.why: Melting only lets the ghee's molecules move more freely. They stay whole, so cooling brings the solid back. Picking 'made new bonds' would mean a new substance, which would not turn back into ghee. Atoms are never destroyed in cooking.

experiments.title: Split Water with a Pencil and a Battery
experiments.context: In this experiment you use a 9-volt battery and two pencils to split water into two gases. Then you test which pencil makes more gas, and why.
experiments.question: Can a battery split water into something that is not water? Which pencil makes more gas, and does it depend on the pencil or on the battery?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the battery is joined, what will you see at the pencil tips? Will both tips do the same thing? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep the same glass, water, soda and pencils all through. Only swap which wire goes to which pencil. If the busier side moves with the black wire, the battery decides it, not the pencil.
results_table: Pencil A: few bubbles, some, or many
Pencil B: few bubbles, some, or many
Which wire was on the busier pencil?

materials.item: a 9-volt battery, the small box-shaped kind, with a snap clip that has a red and a black wire
2 ordinary wooden pencils, sharpened at both ends. If a pencil has a rubber on the end, pull it off or ask a grown-up to cut that end off.
a clear glass or plastic tumbler of tap water
cooking soda (baking soda)
a strip of cardboard, longer than the glass is wide, from a cereal or medicine box
a steel plate or lid, and a cup of hot water from a kettle or pan, for the steam step
a torch or phone light, to see the bubbles better

experiments.safety: Use only a 9-volt battery, never a wall plug or a charger. Do not let the two clip wires touch each other, or the battery gets hot. Keep flames away, because a little hydrogen is made. Do not drink the water. Pour it down the sink afterwards. A grown-up handles the hot water.

schedule.what: Catch steam on a cold plate. Then set up two pencils in soda water, join the battery and compare the bubbles. Swap the wires and compare again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for both tests. Draw the glass, the pencils and the bubbles, and label which wire went where.

flow.do: 1. Pour hot water from a kettle or pan into a cup. 2. Hold a cool steel plate over it for a minute. 3. Let your child touch the drops underneath.
flow.say: First let's see what heat does to water. What are these drops made of?
flow.kid: Look under the plate. Touch a drop. What is it?
flow.parent: Hold the plate yourself, a little above the cup, so steam cannot scald anyone. The drops are water. Heat turned water to steam, and the cool plate turned it back.

ask.q: Did boiling change the water into something new?
good: No, the steam became water again.

flow.context: This is the first step of the water-splitting experiment. You see first that heat does not change water into anything new.

flow.do: 1. Sharpen both pencils at both ends. 2. Poke two holes in the cardboard strip, about 2 cm apart. 3. Push a pencil through each hole. 4. Fill the glass and stir in 1 teaspoon of cooking soda. 5. Lay the strip across the glass, so the tips are in the water.
flow.say: Now let's try something heat cannot do. The pencils' grey lead carries electricity.
flow.kid: Sharpen both pencils at both ends. Push them through the cardboard. Stand them in the soda water. The tips must not touch.
flow.parent: Pencil lead is graphite, a form of carbon, which carries electricity. The soda helps the water carry electricity. The pencil tips should be in the water but not touching each other or the bottom.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before joining the battery.
flow.say: When we join the battery, what do you think will happen at the tips? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: What will happen when the battery is joined? Say why you think so.
flow.parent: Wait for both a guess and a reason. Any guess is fine. Write it down.

flow.do: 1. Snap the clip on the battery. 2. Twist the red wire's bare end round the top lead of one pencil. 3. Twist the black wire round the other. 4. Shine a torch through the glass and watch the tips.
flow.say: Look closely at the bottom of each pencil. What do you see?
flow.kid: Join the red wire to one pencil. Join the black wire to the other. Shine the torch. What is at the tips?
flow.parent: Within a few seconds, tiny bubbles stream up from both tips. If not, check that the wire touches the lead, not the wood, and add a little more soda. Keep the two wires apart.

check.q: The water is bubbling, but it is still cool. What are the bubbles?
options: Steam, because the water is boiling
Air that was hiding in the pencils
check.why: The water is not hot, so it is not boiling, and boiling would only make steam. The battery is splitting water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen gas. Picking 'air in the pencils' is a fair guess. But the bubbles keep coming for as long as the battery is joined, far more than a pencil could hold.

flow.do: 1. Watch both tips for a minute. 2. Decide which tip makes more bubbles. 3. Write it in the table, with the colour of its wire.
flow.say: Do both tips make the same amount of bubbles? Look carefully.
flow.kid: Watch both tips. Which one makes more bubbles? Which wire is on it? Write it down.
flow.parent: The pencil on the black wire, the minus side, usually makes about twice as many bubbles. The bubbles are tiny, so the difference can be hard to see. Use the torch and count for 10 seconds on each side. If both look the same, write that down honestly. That is hydrogen. The red side makes oxygen. The oxygen side may also turn the water a little grey, as bits of lead come off. That is normal.

flow.do: 1. Unhook both wires. 2. Swap them, so red goes where black was. 3. Watch again for a minute and write down which tip is busier now.
flow.say: Is it the pencil that decides, or the battery? Let's swap the wires and find out.
flow.kid: Swap the wires. Watch again. Which tip is busy now?

ask.q: Why do we swap the wires instead of just looking once?
good: To see if it is the pencil or the battery side.
Because one pencil might just be better.

flow.parent: The busy side moves to the other pencil, following the black wire. So the minus side of the battery decides which gas comes off where.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me what you think now, what you saw that shows it, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think, water can be split, but not by heat. What I saw, steam turned back into water, but the battery made bubbles in cool water, and more on the black wire side. Why, water is made of hydrogen and oxygen held tightly together. The battery pulls them apart, and there are two hydrogens in each molecule.

experiments.title: Wax or Sugar: which comes back the same after heating?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up gently heats candle wax and sugar on spoons. You watch which one turns back into what it was when it cools.
experiments.question: When we heat wax and sugar and let them cool, which one comes back as the same stuff?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Both will melt. When they cool down, will each one be the same as before? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of each, the same kind of steel spoon, the same flame and the same height above it. Wax melts quickly and sugar takes longer, because they are different stuff. Cool both on the same plate for the same time.
results_table: What it was like after cooling

materials.item: 2 old steel tablespoons
sugar
candle wax, scraped off a candle with a blunt knife
a gas stove
a kitchen cloth or tongs to hold the spoon
a steel plate to cool the spoons on

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up holds the spoons over the flame. Melted sugar and wax are much hotter than boiling water and stick to skin. The child watches from an arm's length. Heat the wax gently and take it off the flame as soon as it melts, so it never smokes. Let everything cool for 10 minutes before touching.

schedule.what: Look at wax and sugar. A grown-up heats each until it melts, sugar until it browns. Cool them and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw each spoon before heating and after cooling.

flow.do: 1. Put the sugar on one spoon and the wax shavings on the other. 2. Let your child look closely, feel and smell each.
flow.say: Look at both. Feel them. Smell them. What will heat do? Will they come back the same after cooling? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the sugar and the wax. Feel them. Smell them. Guess what will happen, and say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the wax and sugar experiment. You look closely at both before heating, so you can compare later.

flow.do: Hold the wax spoon over a low flame, about 10 cm above it. Take it off as soon as all the wax has melted.
flow.say: Watch the wax. What is it doing?
flow.kid: Watch the wax spoon from a safe place. What happens?
flow.parent: The wax melts into a clear liquid within a minute. Do not let it get hot enough to smoke. Put the spoon on the plate to cool.

flow.do: Hold the sugar spoon over the same low flame at the same height. If the sugar has not melted after 3 minutes, lower the spoon to about 5 cm. Keep heating after it melts, until it turns golden brown. Then put it on the plate.
flow.say: Now the sugar. Watch the colour, and sniff the air.
flow.kid: Watch the sugar from a safe place. Does the colour change? What do you smell?
flow.parent: The sugar melts, then turns yellow, then brown, with a sweet burnt smell and a little steam. Stop at golden brown. If it turns black, it has gone too far, but it still shows the change.

flow.do: 1. Wait 10 minutes for both spoons to cool. 2. Look at both and feel them. 3. Let your child taste a tiny bit of the cool caramel from the sugar spoon. Do not taste the wax.
flow.say: Is the wax wax again? Is the sugar sugar again?
flow.kid: When they are cool, look again. Is the wax like before? Is the sugar white and sweet like before?
flow.parent: The wax is solid white wax again. The sugar is now a hard, brown, glassy lump that tastes slightly bitter. Soak the sugar spoon in hot water to clean it.

check.q: The wax came back as wax, but the sugar became brown caramel. Why?
options: Heat only moved the wax molecules apart, but it broke the sugar's bonds and made new ones
The sugar was heated for longer, so it is still sugar, just darker
The wax was not really heated
check.why: Melting wax only lets its molecules move apart. When it cools they pack together again, so it is wax. The sugar got hot enough to break bonds inside its molecules. The atoms joined in new ways, and some left as steam. So the brown caramel is new stuff. Picking 'still sugar, just darker' misses the new taste and the steam. Those show that new substances were made.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: wax melted and came back as wax, so its molecules stayed whole. Sugar turned brown, smelled different, gave off steam and tasted different, so its atoms made new bonds and new substances.

experiments.title: Plain, Sugar or Soda Water: which splits best?
experiments.context: This experiment uses the pencil-and-battery setup from the water-splitting test. You find out which water carries the battery's electricity best, by counting bubbles.
experiments.question: Does plain water, sugar water or cooking soda water make the most bubbles with the battery?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which glass will bubble the most? Which the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of water in the same kind of glass, filled to the same level. Use 1 teaspoon of sugar in one glass and 1 teaspoon of soda in another. Use the same pencils at the same distance, and the same battery. Watch each for one minute. Rinse the pencils between glasses.
results_table: Bubbles: none, few, some or many

materials.item: the battery, clip, pencils and cardboard strip from the water-splitting test
3 clear glasses of tap water
sugar
cooking soda
labels or a marker

experiments.safety: Use only a 9-volt battery. Keep the wires apart and flames away. Do not drink the water.

schedule.what: Make three glasses: plain, sugar and soda water. Test each with the pencils and battery for one minute.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three glasses with the bubbles you saw.

flow.do: 1. Label three glasses: plain, sugar, soda. 2. Fill each to the same level with tap water. 3. Stir 1 teaspoon of sugar into one, and 1 teaspoon of soda into another.
flow.say: Which glass do you think will bubble most? Why?
flow.kid: Label three glasses. Stir sugar into one and soda into one. Guess which will bubble most, and say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the three-water test. You make three kinds of water to test with the battery.

flow.do: Put the pencils in each glass in turn, join the battery and watch for one minute. Rinse the pencils between glasses.
flow.say: Watch the tips. Count roughly: none, few, some or many?
flow.kid: Put the pencils in the first glass. Join the battery. Watch for one minute. Then the next glass.
flow.parent: Plain tap water makes very few bubbles, maybe none. Sugar water makes about the same. Soda water makes many. Tap water has a few dissolved minerals, which is why it may make a few bubbles at all.

flow.do: Talk about the result.
flow.say: Sugar dissolved and so did soda. Why did only the soda help?
flow.kid: Which glass bubbled most? Sugar and soda both dissolved. Why did only soda help?

check.q: Soda water bubbled a lot, but sugar water hardly bubbled. Why?
options: Soda breaks into charged particles in water, which carry the electricity
Sugar water is too sticky for bubbles
check.why: Cooking soda is made of particles with electric charges. In water they move apart and carry the electricity between the pencils. Sugar dissolves as whole molecules with no charge, so it carries almost none. Picking 'too sticky' is a fair guess, but one teaspoon of sugar barely thickens a glass of water.

activities.title: Pull It Apart: what holds things together?
activities.context: This is a quick activity to start the unit. You try to pull apart everyday things, and wonder what holds them together.

materials.item: a steel spoon, a sheet of paper, a ball of wheat or rice-flour dough, and an ice cube on a plate

schedule.what: Try to pull apart four things. Talk about what holds each one together.

activities.record: Draw the four things in order, from easiest to pull apart to hardest.

flow.do: Give your child each thing in turn and ask them to try to pull it into two pieces with their hands.
flow.say: Try to pull each one apart. Which is easiest? Which is hardest?
flow.kid: Try to pull each thing into two pieces. Which is easy? Which is hard?
flow.context: This is the first step of Pull It Apart. You feel how hard some things hold together.

flow.do: Ask the big question and listen.
flow.say: The spoon is made of tiny atoms. Why don't the atoms just fall apart into dust? What do you think holds them?
flow.kid: A spoon is made of tiny atoms. Why do they stay together? What do you think?

ask.q: What do you think holds the atoms of the spoon together?
good: They hold on to each other.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Write down your child's idea. The unit will come back to it.

activities.title: Build Molecules with Chana and Toothpicks
activities.context: In this activity you build models of molecules. Soaked chana are the atoms and toothpicks are the bonds.

materials.item: kabuli chana (big) and green moong or small dried peas (small), soaked in water overnight
toothpicks (or broken bamboo skewers)
a black marker

activities.safety: Toothpicks are sharp. Push them into the chana away from your fingers. Do not eat the chana afterwards if they have been handled a lot.

schedule.what: The night before, soak the chana and moong. Then build water, oxygen gas and carbon dioxide models.

activities.record: Draw each model and write its name and its letters, like H2O.

flow.do: 1. Let each big chana be an oxygen atom. 2. Let each small moong be a hydrogen atom. 3. Build water: one chana with two moong, each on its own toothpick.
flow.say: Oxygen has two hands, so it gets two toothpicks. Hydrogen has one.
flow.kid: Big chana is oxygen. Small moong is hydrogen. Push in two toothpicks. Put a moong on each. That is water!
flow.context: This is the first step of building molecules. You make a water molecule from chana and moong.
flow.wait: Soak the chana and moong in water the night before.

flow.do: 1. Build oxygen gas: two chana joined by two toothpicks side by side. 2. Colour one chana black with marker for carbon. 3. Build carbon dioxide: the black chana in the middle, joined to an oxygen chana on each side by two toothpicks.
flow.say: Each atom must use all its hands. How does carbon use four hands on only two oxygens?
flow.kid: Join two chana with two toothpicks. That is oxygen gas. Now make a black chana for carbon. Put an oxygen on each side. Use two toothpicks for each.
flow.parent: Carbon dioxide is O, C, O in a straight line, with two bonds on each side. Carbon has four hands, and each oxygen two.

flow.do: Look at all three models together.
flow.say: Which one do you breathe in? Which one do you breathe out? Which one do you drink?
flow.kid: Which one do you breathe in? Which do you breathe out? Which do you drink?

check.q: Your carbon dioxide model has one carbon and two oxygens. How many toothpicks does it use?
check.why: Carbon has four hands. Each oxygen holds it with two, so there are two toothpicks on each side, four in all. Picking 2 leaves two of carbon's hands, and one of each oxygen's, empty.

activities.title: Be the Atoms: act out melting, boiling and splitting
activities.context: In this activity family members act as atoms holding hands. You act out what happens to water when it boils, and when a battery splits it.

materials.item: at least 3 people, or 1 person and 2 soft toys
paper labels: O, H, H

schedule.what: Make a water molecule from people. Act out ice, water, steam and splitting.

activities.record: Draw your family as a water molecule.

flow.do: 1. The oxygen person wears the O label and holds out both hands. 2. Each hydrogen person holds one hand. Their other hand stays by their side.
flow.say: Oxygen has two hands. Hydrogen has one. Now we are a water molecule.
flow.kid: The oxygen holds out two hands. Each hydrogen holds one. You are water!
flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Atoms. You make a water molecule out of people.

flow.do: 1. If you have two families or friends, make two water molecules. 2. Stand close and still for ice. 3. Shuffle slowly past each other for water. 4. Move fast around the room for steam. Never let go of your partners.
flow.say: Now we are boiling. Do the water molecules let go of each other? Do the atoms let go inside the molecule?
flow.kid: Stand still for ice. Shuffle for water. Walk fast for steam. Keep holding hands!
flow.parent: With only one molecule, act it alone: the molecule stands still, shuffles, then moves fast. The point is that the hands stay held through all three.

flow.do: 1. Now the battery comes. The hydrogens let go of the oxygen. 2. The two hydrogens hold each other's hand, making hydrogen gas. 3. With a second water molecule, the two oxygens hold each other with both hands, making oxygen gas.
flow.say: The battery pulls the atoms apart. Now what do the hydrogens do?
flow.kid: The battery pulls you apart! Hydrogens, let go. Now hold each other's hand. You are hydrogen gas!

check.q: When water boils, which hands let go?
options: None. Whole molecules move apart from other molecules
The hydrogens let go of the oxygen
check.why: In boiling, each molecule stays whole, with its hands still held. The molecules only move far apart. Letting go of the oxygen is what the battery does, and it makes new gases.

flow.parent: Oxygen gas needs the oxygens of two water molecules, which takes six people. With only three, act out hydrogen gas, and say that two oxygens would hold each other with both hands.

activities.title: Pencil Sheets: why graphite writes
activities.context: In this activity you find out why a pencil leaves a mark, by lifting graphite off paper with tape.

materials.item: a soft pencil (2B or darker if you have one)
white paper
clear sticky tape

schedule.what: Shade a dark patch of pencil. Rub it, then lift it with tape.

activities.record: Stick the piece of tape in your notebook and write what it shows.

flow.do: Shade a patch about 3 cm square, pressing hard, until it is shiny grey.
flow.say: Shade a dark patch. Then rub your finger on it. What does it feel like?
flow.kid: Shade a dark patch with the pencil. Rub it with your finger. How does it feel?
flow.context: This is the first step of Pencil Sheets. You make a patch of graphite to test.

flow.do: 1. Press a piece of tape on the patch. 2. Peel it off and hold it up to the light.
flow.say: The tape lifted some grey off. What do you think it picked up?
flow.kid: Press tape on the patch. Peel it off. Hold it to the light. What is on it?
flow.parent: Graphite is carbon atoms in flat sheets. Inside each sheet, the bonds are very strong. Between the sheets they hold on weakly, so the sheets slide, feel slippery and peel off.

flow.do: Talk about diamond.
flow.say: Diamond is also pure carbon, but it is the hardest natural material. How can the same atoms be soft and hard?
flow.kid: Diamond is carbon too. But it is very hard. How can that be?

check.q: Why is pencil lead soft but diamond hard, if both are only carbon?
options: The carbon atoms are bonded in different patterns
Diamond has a different kind of atom inside
check.why: In diamond, every carbon holds four others in all directions, making one strong frame. In graphite the carbons make flat sheets that hold each other only weakly. Picking 'a different kind of atom' is a natural guess, but both are pure carbon.

activities.title: New Stuff Hunt in the Kitchen
activities.context: In this activity you look around the kitchen for changes that make new substances, where atoms have made new bonds.

a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Watch a meal being cooked. List changes that make new stuff and changes that do not.

activities.record: Make two lists: Same stuff and New stuff.

flow.say: Is this the same stuff or new stuff? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Watch the cooking from a safe place. For each change, say same stuff or new stuff.
flow.context: This is the first step of the New Stuff Hunt. You look for chemical changes while a meal is cooked.

flow.do: Read the two lists together.
flow.say: Which list is longer? Is most of cooking same stuff or new stuff?
flow.kid: Read your two lists. Which is longer?

good: No, the atoms made new bonds.

projects.context: In this 2-day project you build models of methane, ammonia and hydrogen peroxide, and make a small book about six molecules from your home and your air.

a marker in two colours
6 sheets of paper, folded and stapled into a book
a phone camera, if you have one

projects.safety: Toothpicks are sharp. Push away from your fingers.

schedule.what: The night before, soak the chana and moong. Then build methane and ammonia. Draw or photograph each.

challenges.title: The Faster Bubble Machine
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You change the water-splitting setup to make bubbles come faster.
challenges.problem: With a 9-volt battery and two pencils, the bubbles come slowly. Make a setup that makes bubbles faster, using only the same battery.
constraints: Change one thing at a time, and compare with the first setup.
materials: the battery, clip, pencils and cardboard strip from the water-splitting test
cardboard strips with holes at different distances
general: Put the pencil tips closer together, without touching.
Add more soda, up to 2 teaspoons.
Use warm tap water instead of cold.
creative: Sharpen the pencils longer, so more grey lead touches the water.
Try two steel safety pins in place of the pencils, and watch what happens to the pins after a few minutes.
Use a wider, shallower dish so you can lay the pencils almost flat, with more lead in the water.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own faster bubble machine. Draw it, test it for one minute, and compare it with the first setup.

flow.do: Set up the water-splitting test with 1 teaspoon of soda, and watch for one minute.
flow.say: This is our starting machine. Watch how fast the bubbles come.
flow.kid: Set up the first machine. Watch for one minute. How fast are the bubbles?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Faster Bubble Machine challenge. You watch the starting setup, to compare later.

flow.do: Change one thing at a time: distance, amount of soda, warmth of water. Watch each for a minute.
flow.say: Which change made the bubbles come fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Watch for one minute. Faster or slower? Then try another change.
flow.parent: Closer pencils and more soda both help, because the electricity has an easier path. Do not use salt, even though it would work well.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the best machine.
flow.say: Draw your best machine and say why it works.
flow.kid: Draw your best machine. Say why it was fastest.

challenges.title: Atom Puzzle Pieces
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make cardboard atom pieces that only fit together in real molecules.
challenges.problem: Design cardboard pieces for hydrogen, oxygen and carbon, so that they only join in ways real atoms can. Water should fit together. A hydrogen with two partners should not.
constraints: Use cardboard, scissors and a pencil.
Hydrogen must join to exactly one piece, oxygen to two, carbon to four.
A grown-up helps with the cutting.
general: Give each piece tabs and slots, like a jigsaw: hydrogen one tab, oxygen two slots, carbon four slots.
Use paper clips as hands, with one clip for hydrogen, two for oxygen and four for carbon.
creative: Give carbon four slots on four sides, so methane fits as a cross.
Make double tabs that fit double slots, so carbon dioxide fits too.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own atom pieces. Can you make water, methane and carbon dioxide fit, but no wrong molecule?

flow.do: Draw designs for the three pieces on cardboard.
flow.say: How will you make sure hydrogen can only hold one partner?
flow.kid: Draw a hydrogen, an oxygen and a carbon piece. Hydrogen joins one. Oxygen two. Carbon four.
flow.context: This is the first step of Atom Puzzle Pieces. You design pieces that join like real atoms.

flow.do: Cut out 4 hydrogens, 2 oxygens and 1 carbon. Try building water and methane.
flow.say: Do your pieces only fit the right way?
flow.kid: Cut out your pieces. Build water. Build methane. Do they fit?
flow.parent: Help with the scissors. If a wrong molecule fits, ask your child how to change the design so it cannot.

flow.do: Test with a wrong molecule, such as a chain H, H, O, where the middle hydrogen holds two partners.
flow.say: Try to make a hydrogen hold two partners. Can you?
flow.kid: Try to make a wrong molecule. Does your design stop it?

quiz.p: What holds two atoms together in a bond?
opts: Their electrons, attracted by both atoms at once
quiz.why: A bond is made by electrons that are attracted by the centres of both atoms. That is the electric force. Hooks and glue are old pictures. Atoms have neither.

quiz.p: A water molecule is written H2O. What does that mean?
quiz.why: H stands for hydrogen and O for oxygen. The small 2 says there are two hydrogen atoms. So one water molecule is two hydrogens and one oxygen.

quiz.p: Steam from a pot drips back off the lid as water. What does this show?
opts: Boiling only moves water molecules apart. Each one stays whole.
Boiling splits water into hydrogen and oxygen
quiz.why: If boiling had split water, the gases would not drip back as water. The water molecules only moved apart, and came close again on the cool lid.

quiz.p: A gas stove flame is hot. Why?
opts: The gas atoms make new, strong bonds with oxygen, which gives out energy
Water is splitting inside the flame
The flame is made of hydrogen only
quiz.why: The atoms of the gas bond with oxygen from the air and make carbon dioxide and water. Making strong new bonds gives out energy as heat and light.

quiz.p: Which of these is a chemical change, where new stuff is made?
opts: A dosa turning golden on the tava
quiz.why: In the dosa, molecules break and join in new ways, giving new colour and taste. The others only move molecules apart, and could be undone.

quiz.p: A balcony grill has turned brown and flaky. What has happened to the iron?
opts: Iron atoms have bonded with oxygen, with help from water, and made rust
Iron atoms have turned into paint
The iron has melted and set again
Water has split the iron into hydrogen and oxygen
quiz.why: Rusting makes a new substance. Iron atoms bond with oxygen from the air, and water helps. Melting would only be a change you can undo by cooling.

quiz.p: Diamond and pencil lead are both pure carbon. Why is pencil lead soft?
opts: Its carbon atoms are in flat sheets that slide over each other
quiz.why: Graphite's sheets hold each other only weakly, so they slide off onto paper. In diamond every carbon holds four others in all directions.

quiz.p: Oxygen has two hands and hydrogen has one. Which molecule is not possible?
opts: One hydrogen holding two oxygens with its one hand
Two hydrogens holding each other, H2
Two oxygens holding each other with two hands each
quiz.why: Hydrogen has only one hand, so it cannot hold two partners. The others use every hand exactly once.

quiz.p: When something burns, where do most of its atoms go?
opts: Into the air, as new gases like carbon dioxide and water
They all stay in the ash
quiz.why: Atoms are never destroyed in burning. They bond with oxygen and leave as gases. The ash is only a small part.

quiz.p: Bina, a girl in Class 4 in Guwahati, dissolves sugar in one glass and cooking soda in another. With the battery, the soda water bubbles a lot and the sugar water hardly at all. Why?
opts: Soda splits into charged particles that carry electricity, but sugar molecules have no charge
Sugar stops the pencils working for ever
quiz.why: Charged particles carry the electricity across the water. Sugar dissolves as whole molecules with no charge, so very little electricity flows and few bubbles form.

items.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 3 in Hyderabad, builds a model of a water molecule. Which model is right?
items.why: Water is H2O: one oxygen with two hydrogens held on to it. A strong answer explains that oxygen has two hands.

items.p: A group of atoms held together by bonds is called a ____.
items.why: A molecule is the smallest piece of a substance like water. Water, oxygen gas and sugar are all made of molecules.

items.p: Ice, liquid water and steam are made of three different kinds of molecule.
items.why: False. All three are H2O molecules. Only the spacing and the movement of the molecules change.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could add an example of each.
pairs: the smallest piece of an element
a group of atoms held together
the way two atoms hold on to each other
a tiny particle on the outside of an atom
a substance with only one kind of atom

items.p: Sort each change. Does it make new stuff, or is it the same stuff moved around?
items.a: see items
items.why: Melting, boiling, drying and dissolving only move molecules. Burning, rusting, browning and setting curd make new bonds. A strong answer uses the test: can you get it back just by cooling or drying?

items.p: When rice is cooked, the lid is covered in drops. Explain where the drops came from, and why they are still water.
items.a: Water in the pot boiled into steam. The steam touched the cool lid and turned back into drops. Boiling only moved the water molecules apart, so each one was still water.
items.why: A strong answer says the molecules stayed whole, so the drops are water, not something new.

items.p: Draw a water molecule. Use a big circle for oxygen and small circles for hydrogen. Draw a line for each bond. Label each atom.
items.a: A big circle labelled O, with two small circles labelled H, each joined to the O by one line.
items.why: Oxygen makes two bonds and each hydrogen makes one. A strong drawing has exactly two lines.

items.p: How many bonds does a carbon atom usually make?
items.why: Carbon usually makes four bonds. That is why it can build so many different molecules, including the ones in food and in your body.

items.p: Three of these changes make new stuff. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Ghee melting is the odd one out. It only moves the ghee's molecules apart, and cooling makes it solid again. The other three make new substances.

items.p: Put the steps of the water-splitting test in order.
a: Sharpen two pencils at both ends
Stand them in soda water, not touching
Join the battery's wires to the pencils
Watch which pencil makes more bubbles
items.why: First get the pencils ready, then put them in the water, then join the battery, then watch.
items: Join the battery's wires to the pencils
Watch which pencil makes more bubbles
Sharpen two pencils at both ends
Stand them in soda water, not touching

items.p: Here is a picture of the water-splitting setup. Label the battery, the black wire, the pencil that makes hydrogen and the pencil that makes oxygen.
a: Black wire: joined to the busier pencil
Hydrogen: the pencil on the black wire
Oxygen: the pencil on the red wire
items.why: The minus, black side makes hydrogen and the red side makes oxygen. A strong answer also says which side had more bubbles.
items.art: A drawing of a glass with two pencils, wires to a battery, and four empty label boxes.

items.p: The oxygen in the air is made of pairs of oxygen atoms, held together by bonds.
items.why: True. Each oxygen molecule is two oxygen atoms holding each other with two bonds. It is written O2.

items.p: In your water-splitting test, which pencil made more bubbles? What do you think those bubbles were?
items.a: The pencil on the black wire made more bubbles. They were hydrogen gas. The other pencil made oxygen.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child really saw, and links the extra bubbles to the two hydrogens in each water molecule.

items.p: Match each atom to the number of bonds it usually makes.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Hydrogen makes 1 bond, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3 and carbon 4. A strong answer uses these to explain why water is H2O.

items.p: The tiny particles on the outside of an atom, which make bonds, are called ____.
items.why: Electrons have a negative charge. They are attracted by the positive centres of atoms, and that holds atoms together.

items.p: Two cousins in Kochi watch a grown-up melt wax and sugar on spoons.
items.a: A strong answer uses the evidence: after cooling, the wax was wax again, but the sugar was brown, glassy and tasted different, and gave off steam. So the sugar's atoms made new bonds. It also gives Farhan his due: the atoms of the sugar are all still there, in the caramel and in the steam.
items.why: Both see part of it. The substance sugar is gone, but its atoms are not. A strong answer says both.

views.says: The sugar is gone. Caramel is a new thing.
Nothing is gone. It is still the same sugar, just cooked.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the wax and sugar experiment. Then say one thing the other cousin has right.

items.p: Why is water H2O, and not HO?
items.why: Oxygen has two hands. With only one hydrogen, one of oxygen's hands would be empty. Two hydrogens fill both.
opts: Oxygen makes two bonds and hydrogen makes one
There is more hydrogen in the world

items.p: Methane is the main gas in biogas. It has one carbon atom and some hydrogen atoms. Carbon has four hands and hydrogen has one. How many hydrogens does methane have? Explain.
items.a: Four. Each of carbon's four hands holds one hydrogen, so methane is CH4.
items.why: A strong answer uses the hand numbers to reason, not just recalls the formula.

items.p: Draw carbon dioxide, CO2. Carbon is in the middle and an oxygen is on each side. Draw a line for every bond, so every atom uses all its hands.
items.a: O, C, O in a row, with two lines between the carbon and each oxygen.
items.why: Carbon has four hands and each oxygen has two. So each oxygen holds the carbon with both its hands. A strong drawing shows two double bonds.

items.p: Diamond and pencil lead are both made only of carbon atoms.
items.why: True. They differ because their carbon atoms are bonded in different patterns: a 3D frame in diamond, flat sheets in graphite.

items.p: A pencil leaves a mark on paper, but a diamond can cut glass. Both are carbon. Explain why they behave so differently.
items.a: In pencil lead, carbon atoms are held in flat sheets that hold each other weakly, so the sheets slide off onto paper. In diamond every carbon holds four others in all directions, so it is very hard.
items.why: A strong answer talks about the pattern of bonds, not about different atoms.

items.p: Which takes more energy: boiling a glass of water away, or splitting the same water into hydrogen and oxygen?
items.why: Splitting it takes several times more energy, because it breaks the strong bonds inside each molecule. Boiling only separates whole molecules, which hold each other weakly.

items.p: Sort each change: does it give out heat, or does it need heat put in?
items.a: see items
items.why: Burning makes new strong bonds with oxygen, which gives out heat. Cooking and melting need heat put in, to break bonds or move molecules apart. A strong answer explains one of each.

items.p: Splitting water with electricity is called ____.
items.why: Electro means electricity and lysis means splitting. A 9-volt battery and two pencils can do it.

items.p: Match each molecule to the atoms in it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The letters say which atoms, and the small numbers say how many. A strong answer could check each one with the hand numbers.

items.p: Three of these are made of only one kind of atom. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Water has two kinds of atom, hydrogen and oxygen, so it is a compound. O2, H2 and N2 each have only one kind, so they are elements.

items.p: Two friends in Mysuru look at an old rusty nail.
items.a: A strong answer says that the iron atoms are all still there, now bonded to oxygen, but the shiny metal iron is gone. So both are partly right, and the argument is about whether 'iron' means the atoms or the metal.
items.why: This is a real question about what we mean by a substance. A strong answer separates atoms from the substance they make.

views.says: The iron is still there, just joined to oxygen.
The iron is gone. Rust is a new substance, a brown powder that is not metal.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give your reason. Then say what the other friend has right.

items.p: When atoms make new bonds in a chemical change, some atoms get used up and disappear.
items.why: False. No atoms disappear. They only change partners. Weigh everything in a closed jar before and after, and the weight stays the same.

items.p: Priya stirs sugar into hot tea and it disappears. How could she get the sugar back?
items.why: Dissolving only spreads whole sugar molecules among the water molecules. Let the water dry away and the sugar is left. It was never destroyed.
opts: Let the water dry away, and the sugar is left
She cannot, because dissolving destroys sugar
Freeze the tea until the sugar turns to caramel

items.p: In the water-splitting test, you swapped the wires. Why was that a good idea? What did it show?
items.a: It showed whether the pencil or the battery decided which side made more bubbles. The busier side moved with the black wire, so the battery's minus side decides.
items.why: A strong answer explains that changing only one thing lets you find the cause.

items.p: Put these in order from smallest to biggest.
items.why: An electron is part of an atom. Atoms make up a molecule. A grain of sugar holds a huge number of molecules.

items.p: Draw a box of ice and a box of steam. Show the water molecules in each. Do the molecules change, or only the spaces between them?
items.a: Ice: molecules close together in a neat pattern. Steam: the same H2O molecules far apart. Each molecule stays whole.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps every molecule as one O with two H's in both boxes.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side.

items.p: In 1955, a British chemist called Charles Coulson wrote that nobody has ever seen a bond. In 2009, scientists made a picture of one molecule where the bonds showed up as lines.
items.a: A strong answer weighs both: bonds can be measured and now pictured, but what the pictures show is where electrons gather. It says what would change your mind.
items.why: This is a real argument among chemists. Both sides have evidence.

views.says: A bond is an idea we made up to describe atoms. Only atoms and electrons are real.
A bond is real. We can measure how long it is and how strong it is, and now we can see it.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other side has right.

items.p: Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, is used to clean cuts. It has two hydrogens and two oxygens. Draw it so every atom uses all its hands, and no hydrogen holds two partners.
items.a: H, O, O, H in a chain: each hydrogen holds one oxygen, and the two oxygens hold each other.
items.why: Each oxygen uses one hand for a hydrogen and one for the other oxygen. A strong drawing has three lines.

items.p: Most of the air is nitrogen gas, N2. Nitrogen has three hands. How can two nitrogen atoms hold all their hands with only each other?
items.a: They hold each other with all three hands at once. This is a triple bond.
items.why: A strong answer sees that two atoms can share more than one bond. This triple bond is very strong, which is why nitrogen gas changes so rarely.

items.p: Vikram, a boy in Class 4, draws a molecule as H, H, O in a row: the middle hydrogen holds the other hydrogen and the oxygen. What is wrong with it?
items.why: The middle hydrogen is holding two partners, but hydrogen has only one hand. In real water, both hydrogens hold the oxygen.
opts: The middle hydrogen has two partners, but hydrogen makes only one bond
Oxygen should be at the end

items.p: A candle burns away in a closed jar, and the jar with everything in it weighs the same as before. Where did the wax go, and why does the weight stay the same?
items.a: The wax atoms bonded with oxygen and became carbon dioxide and water vapour inside the jar. No atoms left the jar or were destroyed, so the weight stays the same.
items.why: A strong answer says atoms change partners but are not lost.

items.p: A baked cake could be turned back into flour, sugar and eggs just by cooling it in the fridge.
items.why: False. Baking makes new bonds and new substances. Cooling only slows molecules down. It cannot undo a chemical change.

items.p: Sort these: an element (one kind of atom) or a compound (more than one kind)?
items.a: see items
items.why: Oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen gas, and diamond, each have one kind of atom. Water, carbon dioxide, methane and sugar have two or more kinds.

items.p: For 2,000 years people thought water was an element. Which finding showed that it is not?
items.why: A battery split water into two different gases. An element cannot be split into other substances. Freezing and boiling only change how water molecules move.
opts: A battery splits water into hydrogen and oxygen

items.p: Astronauts on the International Space Station get oxygen to breathe by splitting water with electricity. In your experiment, which pencil gave the gas they breathe? What else do they get?
items.a: The pencil on the red, plus wire gave oxygen. They also get hydrogen, twice as much, from the black wire side.
items.why: A strong answer uses the result of the child's own test.

items.p: When two atoms share electrons in a bond, they are held together by the ____ force.
items.why: Opposite electric charges attract. The positive centres of both atoms attract the shared electrons, and that holds the atoms together.

items.p: A rusty nail weighs a little more than the shiny nail did. Why?
items.why: Oxygen atoms from the air have bonded with the iron atoms. No iron is lost, and the extra atoms add weight.
opts: Oxygen atoms from the air have joined the iron atoms
The nail soaked up heat, and heat has weight

items.p: Match each change to what happens to the molecules.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A strong answer can say which changes break the bonds inside molecules and which do not.
pairs: sugar molecules spread among water molecules
atoms make new bonds with oxygen

items.p: Why did we use pencil lead in the water-splitting test, and not a wooden stick?
items.why: Pencil lead is graphite, a form of carbon that carries electricity. Wood does not carry it well enough.
opts: Graphite is the same as soda

items.p: Many people think heating always breaks things into smaller parts. Plan a test with things from your kitchen to check this idea.
items.a: Heat two things gently, such as ice and sugar, and cool them again. Ice comes back as water, nothing new. Sugar breaks, but it also joins up in new ways to make caramel. So heating can break bonds, but can also make new ones.
items.why: A strong plan compares at least two things and says what result would support or go against the idea.

items.p: The oxygen atoms you breathe in can end up in water that you breathe out.
items.why: True. Your cells use oxygen to get energy from food. The oxygen atoms bond with hydrogen to make water, which leaves your body in your breath, sweat and urine.

items.p: Design a test to show that the bubbles in the water-splitting test are not steam. Draw what you would do and what you would expect to see.
items.a: For example, put a thermometer in the water or feel the glass: it stays cool. Or put an ice cube in the water: the bubbles keep coming.
items.why: A strong design uses a way to check the temperature, since steam needs boiling water.

applications: Making medicines: chemists design molecules atom by atom.
Cooking: heat breaks and makes bonds, which gives food new tastes and colours.
Splitting water with electricity makes hydrogen fuel, and oxygen for space stations.
Cutting tools for stone and glass use diamond, the hardest natural material.
Pencils use soft graphite, whose sheets slide off onto paper.
Fertilisers are made from the nitrogen in air by breaking its strong triple bond.
Biogas plants turn cow dung and food waste into methane for cooking.
Rust-proof paint keeps oxygen from bonding with the iron in gates and grills.

open_questions.why_open: Bonds can be measured and pictured, but chemists still argue whether a bond is a separate thing or just a description of where electrons are.

open_questions.q: How can we split water cheaply, using sunlight?
open_questions.why_open: Plants split water every day with light. Scientists are still trying to build materials that do it as well and as cheaply, to make clean hydrogen fuel.

open_questions.q: Can we predict exactly how any new molecule will behave before making it?
open_questions.why_open: The rules of electrons are known, but the sums for big molecules are so huge that even fast computers must use shortcuts.

open_questions.q: How did the first molecules of life join up on the early Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made some building blocks of life in the lab, but nobody knows how they first joined into living cells.

Why was carbon so popular at the party?

jokes.j: Why didn't the water molecule fall apart in the kettle?
jokes.a: It kept a tight grip on its hydrogens.

jokes.j: What did the sugar say on the hot spoon?

jokes.j: Why did the iron gate turn brown?
