maths.context: This is about the water-splitting test, where two pencils stand in soda water joined to a battery.
maths.problem: Priya, a girl in Class 4 in Coimbatore, counted bubbles leaving each pencil for 10 seconds. The black wire pencil made 24 bubbles. The red wire pencil made 12. How many times as many bubbles did the black side make?
maths.explain: 24 divided by 12 is 2. So the black side made twice as many bubbles. That fits, because each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one count by the other shows the pattern, two to one, that matches the H2O formula.

maths.context: This is about building molecules with soaked chana for oxygen and moong for hydrogen.
maths.problem: Shalini, a girl in Class 3 in Bhubaneswar, wants to build 3 water molecules with chana and moong. How many chana and how many moong does she need?
maths.explain: Each water molecule is 1 oxygen and 2 hydrogens. 3 groups of 1 is 3 chana. 3 groups of 2 is 6 moong.
maths.why_maths: Each molecule is an equal group of atoms, so multiplying tells you how many atoms any number of molecules needs.

maths.context: This is about table sugar. One sugar molecule is written C12H22O11.
maths.problem: A sugar molecule has 12 carbon atoms, 22 hydrogen atoms and 11 oxygen atoms. How many atoms is that in all?
maths.explain: 12 + 22 = 34. 34 + 11 = 45. So one sugar molecule has 45 atoms, compared with 3 in water.
maths.why_maths: Adding the atoms shows how much bigger a sugar molecule is than a water molecule.

maths.context: This is about atom hands. Hydrogen has 1 hand, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3 and carbon 4. Every bond uses two hands, one from each atom.
maths.problem: Methane is 1 carbon and 4 hydrogens. Count all the hands. How many bonds does methane have?
maths.explain: Carbon has 4 hands and the 4 hydrogens have 1 each, so 8 hands in all. Each bond uses 2 hands. 8 divided by 2 is 4 bonds.
maths.why_maths: Halving the number of hands gives the number of bonds, for any molecule. It also tells you when a molecule is impossible: an odd number of hands means one is left empty.

maths.context: This is about atom hands, as in the Hold Every Hand game.
maths.problem: Rohan, a boy in Class 3, has 1 oxygen card and 1 hydrogen card. Can he build a molecule where every hand is held? Use the hands to explain.
maths.explain: Oxygen has 2 hands and hydrogen has 1, so 3 hands in all. Each bond uses 2 hands. 3 is odd, so one hand is always left empty.
maths.why_maths: Odd and even numbers tell you quickly whether all the hands can be paired.

roots.context: We have learned that atoms hold on to each other with bonds, and that a battery can split water. Now we ask what that tells us about the world and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Steam from hot water dripped back off your plate as water. Your battery split cool water into two gases instead. So the atoms inside water hold on far more tightly than water holds to water. That is why water stays water through ice, rain and steam.
deep_truth.habit: We think of water as one simple stuff, and of heat as the strongest way to change things. People called water an element for over two thousand years, because heat never broke it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the water-splitting test, steam caught on a cool plate turned back into water. A 9-volt battery made hydrogen and oxygen bubbles in cool water, twice as much on the black wire side.

three.who_am_i: More than half of your body's weight is water. Every one of those water molecules is three atoms holding on tight.
three.what_is_life: Living things build their bodies by making and breaking bonds all day. A plant splits water with sunlight, and you put the atoms back together when you breathe.
three.what_is_this_world: Only 118 kinds of atom make up everything you see. The world's variety comes from how they hold on to each other.

roots.thread: Atoms of only a few kinds join, by their bonds, into countless different molecules. Every bond is made by the same electric force. The hydrogen in water and the hydrogen in sugar are the same kind of atom, held in different company. So the many substances around us are a few kinds of atom, held together by one force in different ways.

teachings.source: Prashastapada, Padarthadharmasangraha (about the 6th century CE), on the Vaisheshika teaching of Kanada
teachings.teaching: Two paramanu, the smallest particles, join to make a pair. Three pairs join to make the smallest thing the eye can see, a speck floating in a sunbeam.
teachings.link: The Vaisheshika thinkers said visible things are built from tiny particles joining in small groups. That is close to what molecules are, though they did not know about electrons.

teachings.teaching: Love brings the elements together into one, and Strife pulls them apart again, over and over.
teachings.link: Empedocles thought water was an element, which turned out to be wrong. But his picture of one force joining and another parting fits what you saw: bonds hold atoms together, and energy from a battery or a flame pulls them apart.

science.text: Every chemical bond is made by electrons attracted by two atoms' centres at once. This is the electric force, the same force that makes a balloon stick to a wall.
Since 2009, special microscopes have made pictures of single molecules in which the bonds show up as lines.

other_view.who: Charles Coulson, a British chemist, and many physicists
other_view.view: A bond is not a thing in itself. There are only atoms and electrons, and 'bond' is our word for where the electrons gather. Calling it holding hands is a helpful picture, not a fact.

practice.title: Hold on, let go
practice.say: Let's sit in a circle and hold hands. Close your eyes. Feel the grip of the hands on each side of you. Now let go, and rest your hands on your knees. Breathe in slowly. Some oxygen atoms you breathe in will join with hydrogen inside you to make water. Breathe out. Now hold hands again.
practice.kid: Hold someone's hand. Feel the grip. Let go. Breathe in slowly. Some of that oxygen will become water inside you. Breathe out.

ask: If a bond is made of electrons that both atoms share, which atom do those electrons belong to?
Water is two gases holding on. Is water a new thing, or only hydrogen and oxygen together?
When your body makes water from the oxygen you breathe, is that water part of you or part of the world?
roots.art: A family sitting in a circle holding hands on a living-room floor, with faint drawings of water molecules floating around them.

how_we_found_out.story: For over two thousand years, many thinkers in Greece and elsewhere said water was an element, one of the basic stuffs that could not be split. In 1766, the English scientist Henry Cavendish made a gas that burned easily, which he called inflammable air. In 1781 he burned it in air, and found that dew formed: the only thing made was water. In France, Antoine Lavoisier repeated this. His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, kept the notes of their experiments and drew the equipment for his book. Lavoisier named the gas hydrogen, meaning 'water maker'. He said water was not an element, but hydrogen joined to oxygen. Some scientists still doubted it. Then in 1800, soon after Alessandro Volta described the first battery, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle in London put two wires from a battery into water. Bubbles of gas rose from the wires, and the water was not boiling. Later tests showed one gas was hydrogen and the other oxygen, with twice as much hydrogen. Water had been split, so it could not be an element.
how_we_found_out.who: Henry Cavendish, an English scientist; Antoine and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier in Paris; and William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle in London
how_we_found_out.when: 1766 and 1781 (Cavendish), the 1780s (the Lavoisiers), and 1800 (Nicholson and Carlisle)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed water was an element that could not be split into anything else. Cavendish and Lavoisier made water by burning hydrogen in air, and Nicholson and Carlisle split water into two gases with a battery.

playtest: Every activity and experiment was walked through on paper against the materials list, not tried in a kitchen. The water-splitting test uses a standard home setup: a 9-volt battery, pencils sharpened at both ends and cooking soda in water. It gives visible bubbles within seconds, more at the minus side. Salt is moved out of the main test because it makes a little chlorine. The sugar test uses a gas stove and is grown-up only. The candle wax is warmed gently and taken off as soon as it melts, so it never smokes.
